law.label: Law 91/1992, art. 3-bis (added by Decree-Law 36/2025, converted by Law 74/2025)

fee.label: Consular fee for recognition, per adult

usdFee.label: Same fee in dollars at the New York consulate, October 1 to December 31, 2026

time.text: 730 days legal limit (24 months at San Francisco); 36 months for adult files under Law 11/2026

dual.text: No renunciation of US citizenship (art. 11 of Law 91/1992).

it.gens: Parent or grandparent only, since March 28, 2025

feeReacq.label: Reacquisition by declaration under art. 17, at a consulate

ie.name: Ireland

law.label: Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, s. 7 (as amended)

fee.label: Foreign Birth Registration, applicant 18 or over (EUR 270 + EUR 8 postage)

time.text: about 12 months for a complete application, in strict date order

gb.name: United Kingdom
gb.authority: UK Visas and Immigration (online forms UKM, UKF, MN1)

fee.label: Registration under s. 4C (form UKM) or as child of an unmarried father (UKF): citizenship ceremony fee only

feeChild.label: Registering a child under s. 3(2) (form MN1)

feeStatus.label: Confirmation that you are already British (form NS)

feePriority.label: Optional priority service (about 30 working days), applicants inside the UK only

dual.text: Dual citizenship is allowed in the UK.

pl.name: Poland

law.label: Polish Citizenship Act of 2 April 2009, with the 1920 and 1951 Acts for earlier births

pl.authority: a Polish consulate in the US, which forwards the file to a voivode (regional governor) in Poland

time.text: no decision time published by the voivodes

dual.text: Tolerated: Poland treats a dual citizen solely as Polish on its territory.

restore.label: Restoration of Polish citizenship lost before January 1, 1999 (2009 Act, art. 38), decided by the Minister of the Interior

ca.name: Canada

law.label: Citizenship Act, s. 3, as amended by Bill C-3 (S.C. 2025, c. 5)

ca.authority: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (proof of citizenship certificate)

time.text: not published for certificates on the pages read; a citizenship record search is shown at 19 months (October 21, 2026)

dual.text: Canada allows multiple citizenship; you need a Canadian passport to fly back to Canada.

ca.gens: No limit for people born before December 15, 2025; after that, 1,095 days of the parent's presence in Canada

feeSearch.label: Search for your record of citizenship

law.label: Norwegian Nationality Act 2005, ss. 4, 22 a and 24

no.authority: the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI), through a Norwegian mission in the US

fee.label: Getting Norwegian citizenship back by notification, adult

feeStandard.label: Standard application for Norwegian citizenship, adult

dual.text: No renunciation for s. 58c, but acquiring another citizenship after filing costs Austrian citizenship retroactively; outside s. 58c Austria generally forbids dual citizenship.

gr.authority: the Greek consulate for your US address, which registers you in a municipal register in Greece

fee.label: Registration of a person Greek from birth: no fee in the Code

hu.authority: the Hungarian consulate for your US address (citizenship verification or simplified naturalization)

time.text: several months for a verification (New York consulate); 3 months, extendable by 3, for the minister's step of a naturalization

dual.text: No renunciation of US citizenship is asked, but a Slovak citizen who later naturalizes abroad loses it, save exceptions.

lt.name: Lithuania

lt.authority: the Migration Department, online in MIGRIS, with originals at a Lithuanian consulate

dualTable.name: Argentina
dualTable.note: An Argentine who naturalizes in a country without a dual-nationality agreement is treated as Argentine for all purposes; the agreement with the US applied only until October 20, 1981.

dualTable.name: Armenia
dualTable.note: Obtaining another citizenship does not automatically end Armenian citizenship, which is granted or renounced only by presidential decree.
dualTable.descent: Adults who are ethnic Armenians by descent can acquire citizenship without residence, proving ancestry with a baptism certificate, a foreign document recording Armenian descent, or a parent's, grandparent's or sibling's ID showing Armenian ancestry, plus kinship records.

dualTable.name: Australia
dualTable.note: Australians have been able to take another citizenship without losing Australian citizenship since April 4, 2002; adults who did so before that date may have lost it under old s. 17.

dualTable.name: Austria
dualTable.note: No renunciation for s. 58c, but acquiring another citizenship after filing costs Austrian citizenship retroactively; outside s. 58c Austria generally forbids dual citizenship.
dualTable.descent: Parent only at birth; no limit for descendants of persecuted people (s. 58c)

dualTable.name: Belgium
dualTable.note: Since April 28, 2008 a Belgian who voluntarily acquires US citizenship keeps Belgian nationality; before June 9, 2007 it was lost.
dualTable.descent: Belgians born abroad after January 1, 1967 who did not mainly live in Belgium between 18 and 28 lose Belgian nationality on their 28th birthday unless they file a declaration to keep it.

dualTable.name: Brazil
dualTable.note: Since Constitutional Amendment 131/2023 a Brazilian loses nationality only on express request (or cancelled naturalization), so taking US citizenship no longer costs Brazilian nationality.
dualTable.descent: A child born abroad to a Brazilian father or mother is a native Brazilian if registered at a competent Brazilian office, or if they come to live in Brazil and opt for Brazilian nationality (art. 12, I, c).

dualTable.name: Canada
dualTable.note: Canada allows multiple citizenship; you need a Canadian passport to fly back to Canada.
dualTable.descent: No limit for people born before December 15, 2025; after that, 1,095 days of the parent's presence in Canada

dualTable.name: China
dualTable.note: China does not recognize dual nationality; a Chinese national settled abroad who naturalizes in the US loses Chinese nationality automatically.
dualTable.descent: A child born abroad to a Chinese parent is Chinese, except when a Chinese parent has settled abroad and the child acquired a foreign nationality at birth (art. 5), which covers most US-born children.

dualTable.name: Colombia
dualTable.note: Colombian nationality is not lost by acquiring US or any other nationality (Constitution art. 96).

dualTable.name: Croatia
dualTable.note: Acquiring US citizenship does not end Croatian citizenship, which ends only by release, renunciation or treaty; Croatian authorities treat a dual national solely as Croatian.

dualTable.name: Czech Republic
dualTable.note: Since January 1, 2014 Czech citizens keep their citizenship when they take another.
dualTable.descent: Children and grandchildren of a former citizen (declaration)

dualTable.name: Denmark
dualTable.note: Since September 1, 2015 a Dane who takes US citizenship keeps Danish citizenship.

dualTable.name: Dominican Republic
dualTable.note: Dominicans may acquire a foreign nationality, and acquiring it does not mean losing Dominican nationality (Constitution art. 20).
dualTable.descent: Children born abroad to a Dominican mother or father are Dominican even if they hold another nationality by birthplace; at 18 they may declare that they assume dual nationality or renounce one (art. 18.4).

dualTable.name: El Salvador
dualTable.note: Salvadorans by birth have the right to dual or multiple nationality and lose it only by express renunciation (Constitution art. 91).
dualTable.descent: Children of a Salvadoran father or mother born abroad are Salvadorans by birth (art. 90, 2º).

dualTable.name: Finland
dualTable.note: Finland has allowed multiple citizenship since the Nationality Act 359/2003 came into force on June 1, 2003; the Act has no rule ending Finnish citizenship on naturalization abroad.
dualTable.descent: A child of a Finnish mother is Finnish at birth, and of a Finnish father if married to the mother (as enacted in 2003); a Finn who also holds another citizenship keeps Finnish citizenship at 22 only with sufficient ties to Finland (s. 34).

dualTable.name: France
dualTable.note: No renunciation of US citizenship; French nationals who take another nationality keep French nationality unless they declare otherwise.
dualTable.descent: No limit in law, but blocked after 50 years abroad without French papers (art. 30-3)

dualTable.name: Germany
dualTable.note: Accepted generally since June 27, 2024; losses before that date stay.
dualTable.descent: No limit, if every link was still German when the next child was born

dualTable.name: Greece
dualTable.note: Taking another citizenship does not end Greek citizenship without the Interior Minister's permission.
dualTable.descent: No limit, generation by generation, each one registered in Greece

dualTable.name: Hungary
dualTable.note: Hungary does not ask you to give up US citizenship.
dualTable.descent: No limit for simplified naturalization, with a conversation in Hungarian

dualTable.name: India
dualTable.note: Indian citizenship ends automatically when an Indian acquires US citizenship (Citizenship Act s. 9); the Indian passport must be surrendered. OCI is a visa status, not dual citizenship.

dualTable.name: Ireland
dualTable.note: Ireland allows dual citizenship.
dualTable.descent: Parent born in Ireland (automatic) or grandparent born in Ireland (register)

dualTable.name: Italy
dualTable.note: No renunciation of US citizenship (art. 11 of Law 91/1992).
dualTable.descent: Parent or grandparent only, since March 28, 2025

dualTable.name: Jamaica
dualTable.note: Jamaicans do not lose Jamaican citizenship by becoming citizens of another country, as stated by the government information service; renunciation is a formal, voluntary declaration.

dualTable.name: Japan
dualTable.note: A Japanese national who acquires US citizenship by choice, for example by naturalization, loses Japanese nationality automatically; people dual from birth must choose by 20 if dual before 18.
dualTable.descent: A child of a Japanese parent is Japanese at birth, but a child born abroad who also gets a foreign nationality at birth loses Japanese nationality unless a parent files a reservation of Japanese nationality with the birth notification within 3 months.

dualTable.name: Latvia
dualTable.note: Exiles and their descendants keep any citizenship; others may keep the US one, as a NATO country.
dualTable.descent: Any generation, from a citizen on June 17, 1940

dualTable.name: Lithuania
dualTable.note: US citizenship can be kept only if the ancestor was exiled or left Lithuania before March 11, 1990; otherwise it must be renounced.
dualTable.descent: Children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren of a citizen before June 15, 1940

dualTable.name: Mexico
dualTable.note: A Mexican by birth cannot lose Mexican nationality; you enter and leave Mexico as a Mexican.
dualTable.descent: No limit since May 18, 2021: each generation registers in turn

dualTable.name: Netherlands
dualTable.note: An adult Dutch citizen who voluntarily takes US citizenship loses Dutch citizenship unless one of three exceptions applies (born and living in the US, 5 years' US residence as a minor, or spouse's citizenship); a US-born child who is Dutch from birth keeps both.

dualTable.name: New Zealand
dualTable.note: New Zealand allows dual or multiple citizenship.

dualTable.name: Norway
dualTable.note: Allowed since January 1, 2020.
dualTable.descent: Parent only, Norwegian when you were born

dualTable.name: Philippines
dualTable.note: The Philippines allows dual citizenship, but a natural-born Filipino who naturalized in the US must retain or reacquire Philippine citizenship by oath under RA 9225; it is not automatic.

dualTable.name: Poland
dualTable.note: Tolerated: Poland treats a dual citizen solely as Polish on its territory.
dualTable.descent: No limit, if every link was still Polish when the next child was born

dualTable.name: Portugal
dualTable.note: No renunciation required; Portuguese nationality ends only by a declaration of the person.
dualTable.descent: Parent, or grandparent with a language and culture test since May 19, 2026

dualTable.name: Romania
dualTable.note: Romanian citizenship is lost only by withdrawal, approved renunciation or other cases set by law, not by taking US citizenship.
dualTable.descent: Former citizens who lost Romanian citizenship for reasons not attributable to them, and their descendants up to the third degree, can regain or be granted it and keep their foreign citizenship (art. 11).

dualTable.name: Singapore
dualTable.note: Singapore does not allow adult citizens to keep another citizenship: the Constitution provides for deprivation on acquiring a foreign citizenship, and ICA's renunciation route is for citizens 21 or older who have acquired another country's citizenship.

dualTable.name: Slovakia
dualTable.note: No renunciation of US citizenship is asked, but a Slovak citizen who later naturalizes abroad loses it, save exceptions.
dualTable.descent: Parent, grandparent or great-grandparent born in Slovakia (discretionary grant)

dualTable.name: Slovenia
dualTable.note: Slovenian law has no automatic loss when a Slovenian citizen acquires US citizenship.

dualTable.name: South Korea
dualTable.note: A Korean who voluntarily acquires US citizenship loses Korean nationality at acquisition; dual nationality from birth is tolerated within the nationality-choice system.
dualTable.descent: A person whose father or mother is a Korean national at the time of the person's birth is Korean at birth (Nationality Act art. 2), and must then choose under the choice system.

dualTable.name: Spain
dualTable.note: An option under art. 20 requires a declaration renouncing US nationality before Spanish authorities; Spaniards by origin keep both.
dualTable.descent: Parent born in Spain (option at any age); grandchildren only through the Democratic Memory Law, closed on October 22, 2025

dualTable.name: Sweden
dualTable.note: Allowed since July 1, 2001.
dualTable.descent: Parent only, Swedish when you were born

dualTable.name: Switzerland
dualTable.note: Switzerland has accepted dual nationality without restriction since January 1, 1992; a Swiss citizen who becomes a US citizen keeps Swiss citizenship.

dualTable.name: Ukraine
dualTable.note: Since Law 4502-IX of June 18, 2025, an adult Ukrainian loses citizenship by voluntarily taking another one only if it is an aggressor state's or a state whose citizens cannot use Ukraine's simplified procedure; whether the US is on that list was not checked.
dualTable.descent: A person whose parents, or one parent, were Ukrainian citizens at the time of birth is a Ukrainian citizen, wherever born (art. 7).

dualTable.name: United Kingdom
dualTable.note: Dual citizenship is allowed in the UK.
dualTable.descent: One generation born abroad (a parent born in the UK)

dualTable.name: Vietnam
dualTable.note: Vietnam's default is a single nationality unless the nationality law provides otherwise; since July 1, 2025 some applicants may keep a foreign nationality with close Vietnamese relatives and the President's permission.
